orders.description: Appeal No. 1: Portage and Baldwin’s November 14, 2016 order.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied summary judgment dismissing the amended complaint and on common-law and contractual indemnification cross claims.

orders.description: Appeal No. 2: Tops’ separately appealed summary-judgment order, expressly addressed in the shared memorandum; date unstated.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff slipped and fell on ice in a shopping-center parking lot owned by Portage and managed by Baldwin. Dollar Tree and Tops were tenants sharing that parking lot; plaintiff reported seeing ice around her after the fall.

legal_issues.finding: Portage and Baldwin did not establish absence of retained control; the lease independently raised a triable issue concerning landlord maintenance of common parking areas.
The court expressly noted plaintiffs did not allege creation by Portage, Baldwin or Tops, narrowing the motions to constructive notice; no creation finding was made.
Actual notice was expressly not alleged; the court addressed that limitation rather than deciding actual knowledge.

Defendants failed their initial burden: testimony raised visibility issues, and submissions left a triable issue whether the ice existed long enough to discover and remedy. Constructive notice was not conclusively established.
Tops raised a storm-in-progress argument for the first time in reply; it was procedurally rejected without a storm merits determination.
The out-of-possession defense failed on retained-control proof; even assuming no control, the lease raised an issue concerning contractual maintenance duties.
Conditional indemnification first raised in the appellate reply brief and the storm defense first raised in motion reply papers were not properly before the respective courts.
Portage and Baldwin failed to establish entitlement to common-law or contractual indemnification against Tops; safe maintenance or relinquishment of the duty was not shown.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff’s deposition described surrounding ice; defendants submitted it and it raised visibility issues.
Baldwin’s commercial administration manager testified; the submissions did not establish that control had not been retained.
Plaintiffs submitted the lease requiring landlord maintenance of common areas including parking areas.

The negligence dismissal denials favor plaintiff; the indemnification denial also benefits codefendant Tops. Ancillary indemnification and preservation issues do not displace substantive negligence review. Visibility here concerns constructive notice, not an open-and-obvious defense. Ownership and shared use of the actual lot are explicit; plaintiff’s role and accident date are unstated. A related appeal may require later family handling, but no outside case or prior label was consulted.

evidence.quote: It is hereby ordered that the order so appealed from is unanimously affirmed without costs.

Memorandum: Plaintiffs commenced this action seeking damages for injuries sustained by Harpal Sodhi (plaintiff) when she slipped and fell on ice in the parking lot of a shopping center . Defendant Portage Center, LLC (Portage) is a real estate holding company and the owner of the premises, and defendant Baldwin Real Estate Corporation (Baldwin) is the property manager of the premises. Defendant Dollar Tree Stores, Inc. (Dollar Tree) and defendant Tops Markets, LLC (Tops) were tenants in the shopping center where the incident occurred, and they shared the parking lot in which plaintiff fell .

In appeal No. 1, Portage and Baldwin appeal from an order denying their motion seeking summary judgment dismissing the amended complaint against them and seeking summary judgment on their cross claims against Tops for common-law indemnification and contractual indemnification. In appeal No. 2, Tops appeals from an order denying its motion for summary judgment dismissing the amended complaint against it. We affirm in both appeals.
We note at the outset that plaintiffs did not allege that Portage, Baldwin and Tops (collectively, defendants) created the icy condition or had actual notice of its existence.

In support of their motions, defendants submitted plaintiff's deposition testimony that she observed "ice all around [her]" after she fell, which presented a question of fact whether the icy condition was visible and apparent
Here, defendants' submissions raised a triable issue of fact regarding whether the icy condition existed for a sufficient length of time for the defendants to discover and remedy it

the evidence submitted by Portage and Baldwin, which included testimony of Baldwin's commercial administration manager, failed to establish that Baldwin and Portage had not retained control of the premises

Furthermore, even assuming, arguendo, that Portage and Baldwin established that they did not retain control of the premises, plaintiffs raised a triable issue of fact in opposition by submitting a lease agreement between Portage's predecessor and Dollar Tree, which provided that the "Landlord" was required to maintain "Common Areas" of the premises, including "parking areas."

We reject the contention of Portage and Baldwin that they are entitled to summary judgment on their cross claim for common-law indemnification inasmuch as they failed to establish that Portage complied with its duty to maintain the parking lot in a reasonably safe condition or that it relinquished that duty to Tops
Portage and Baldwin also failed to establish as a matter of law that they were entitled to contractual indemnification

Furthermore, the alternative contention of Portage and Baldwin that the court should have granted judgment on their cross claims "on a conditional basis" was raised for the first time in a reply brief and is therefore not properly before us on appeal
Finally, Tops' contention in appeal No. 2 that there was a storm in progress was raised for the first time in its reply papers and thus was not properly before Supreme Court

Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Niagara County (Richard C. Kloch, Sr., A.J.), entered November 14, 2016. The order denied the motion of defendants Portage Center, LLC, and Baldwin Real Estate Corporation for summary judgment.

orders.description: Shop-Rite’s appeal from the January 14, 2013 denial of dismissal against it.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on water in the produce aisle of Shop-Rite’s supermarket. She testified that after falling she saw an employee nearby unloading produce from a leaking box that was creating the puddle she said she had stepped in.

legal_issues.finding: Shop-Rite made an initial showing of noncreation, but plaintiff’s account of an employee unloading a leaking produce box raised a triable creation issue; no final negligence finding was made.
Shop-Rite’s prima facie showing included lack of notice, without specifying subtypes or notice proof. The triable issue identified in opposition concerned creation.
The court credited an initial lack-of-notice showing without separate duration or inspection analysis; plaintiff’s creation evidence defeated summary judgment.
Plaintiff linked the puddle she stepped in to the leaking box being unloaded by an employee, supporting an inference of creation of the fall-causing condition.
Unsigned deposition transcripts could be considered because they were certified, relied on by Shop-Rite and not challenged as inaccurate.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff’s certified unsigned deposition transcripts were considered and supported the creation inference.

quality.notes: The actual produce aisle and Shop-Rite employee activity establish private retail control; title or lease status is not specified. Plaintiff’s customer role is not inferred solely from being in a supermarket. No accident date, expert, photographs or distinct notice records are stated. Notice is described generically; subtype entries preserve that limitation. The prima facie defense showing is not the final result because plaintiff raised a creation issue.

evidence.quote: Order, Supreme Court, Bronx County (Lizbeth Gonzalez, J.), entered January 14, 2013, which denied the motion of defendant Shop-Rite Supermarkets Inc. (Shop-Rite) for summary judgment dismissing the complaint as against it, unanimously affirmed, without costs.

Shop-Rite established entitlement to judgment as a matter of law in this action where plaintiff alleges that she was injured when she slipped and fell on water on the floor of the produce aisle in Shop-Rite’s supermarket.
Shop-Rite submitted evidence showing that it neither created the subject water condition nor *484 had notice of it
In opposition, plaintiff raised a triable issue of fact as to whether Shop-Rite created the subject condition.

Reliance upon plaintiffs unsigned deposition transcripts in opposing the motion was proper, since the transcripts were certified by court reporters, and Shop-Rite, which relied upon the same transcripts, did not challenge the testimony as inaccurate

Plaintiff testified that after she fell she was wet and noticed a Shop-Rite employee two feet away unloading produce from boxes, one of which was leaking and creating the puddle in which she claimed to have stepped before her fall. Such testimony allows the inference that Shop-Rite created the condition that caused plaintiff to fall

orders.description: Kimieck’s limited appeal from the July 23, 2020 cross-claim ruling.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied dismissal of the owner’s contribution and common-law/contractual indemnification cross-claims; dismissal of plaintiff’s complaint against Kimieck was not appealed.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on ice on exterior stairs at the housing complex where she resided. Wainco owned the premises and retained Kimieck for snow removal; residence is stated without specifying a tenancy.

legal_issues.finding: Showing no duty to plaintiff did not alone negate a duty of reasonable care owed to the owner or dispose of the owner’s cross-claims.
The snow contractor relied solely on lack of duty to plaintiff; that showing was insufficient as to contribution and indemnification claims between defendants.
New appellate arguments were generally unpreserved. The statutory enforceability argument alone qualified for the pure-law exception and was considered.

Kimieck failed the distinct contribution and common-law/contractual indemnification showings. The alternative indemnification clause did not indemnify the owner’s own negligence and was not unenforceable under General Obligations Law § 5-322.1.

evidence_discussed.description: Snow removal contract and its alternative indemnification provision were discussed; the provision did not cover the owner’s own negligence.

quality.notes: Definite third-party-only exclusion: the only appealed branch concerned claims between owner and snow contractor. The unappealed dismissal of plaintiff’s complaint is history, not a second appealed order or mixed appellate result. Affirmance benefits owner Wainco against codefendant Kimieck, so favors=defendant; it is not a negligence recovery for plaintiff. Residence does not establish tenancy. The indemnity statute is not coded as a premises code violation. No creation, notice or storm merits analysis is inferred from the underlying ice fall. This preliminary test-period case is assessed under unchanged rules.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs.
The plaintiff allegedly was injured when she slipped and fell on ice on exterior stairs of the housing complex where she resided.

The premises was owned by the defendant Wainco Goshen 1031, LLC (hereinafter the owner). The owner contracted with the defendant Kimieck Landscaping, Inc. (hereinafter Kimieck), to provide snow removal services for the complex.

In an order dated July 23, 2020, the Supreme Court granted that branch of Kimieck's motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it and denied that branch of its motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the cross-claims asserted against it. Kimieck appeals from so much of the order as denied that branch of its motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the cross-claims asserted against it.

In order to demonstrate its entitlement to summary judgment dismissing the cross-claim for contribution, Kimieck was required to demonstrate, prima facie, not only that it owed no duty to the plaintiff, but that it owed no duty of reasonable care to the owner, independent of its contractual obligations to that party

To obtain summary judgment dismissing the cross-claim for common-law indemnification, Kimieck was required to show, prima facie, that the owner's liability, if any, would be based on the owner's actual wrongdoing, and not on vicarious liability for Kimieck's conduct

Kimieck did not make any of these showings, but instead, relied solely upon its showing that it had no duty to the plaintiff to support its entitlement to summary judgment dismissing the cross-claims.
On appeal, Kimieck makes additional arguments pertaining to the cross-claims. However, these contentions, raised for the first time on appeal, are not properly before this Court
only Kimieck's contention that the indemnification provision of the snow removal contract is unenforceable pursuant to General Obligations Law § 5-322.1 qualifies for that exception.

Since the alternative indemnification provision in the contract does not purport to indemnify the owner for its own negligence, the provision is not unenforceable pursuant to General Obligations Law § 5-322.1
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied that branch of Kimieck's motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the cross-claims asserted against it.

orders.description: Plaintiff’s appeal from the March 5, 2012 summary-judgment dismissal.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on black ice on premises described as defendant’s property and attributed it to water dripping from an ice-filled defective gutter. He testified to drizzle for three to five days before, and at the time of, the accident; the property type and exact fall location are unstated.

legal_issues.finding: Defendant established noncreation; plaintiff failed to raise a factual issue because attributing the ice to gutter runoff amid the described weather would be speculative.
Defendant established lack of actual notice and plaintiff raised no triable issue; the underlying notice proof is not detailed.
Defendant established lack of constructive notice and plaintiff raised no triable issue; no inspection timing or duration analysis is supplied.

The court found the gutter-runoff explanation speculative given the weather and competing possible causes. This concerns the source of the ice, not a failure to identify ice as the alleged slipping condition.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff’s deposition described drizzle before and during the accident; no weather records were identified.

quality.notes: The bare description defendant’s property does not specify private title/control, a house/business use, or the accident area’s boundary. Personal defendant identity and the presence of a gutter do not resolve that gap. The affirmed substantive dismissal is clear, but the binary label stays null pending property review. Do not infer a storm-in-progress holding from drizzle: the actual rationale concerns speculative gutter causation and creation/notice. No expert or weather records, accident date, injured role, or precise defendant legal role is supplied. The other hazard denotes the alleged defective gutter, not a proven defect.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.

The plaintiff commenced this action after he allegedly slipped and fell on “black ice” on the defendant’s property. The plaintiff alleged that water was dripping onto the area where the alleged hazardous condition was located as a result of a defective and *801 unnecessary gutter, which was full of ice.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (Woodard, J.), dated March 5, 2012, which granted the defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
The plaintiff testified at his deposition that it had been drizzling for three to five days prior to his accident, and that it was drizzling at the time of the accident.

Here, the defendant established his prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by demonstrating that he did not create the alleged hazardous condition or have actual or constructive notice of it

In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact. Given the weather conditions at the time of the accident, it would require impermissible speculation to conclude that the ice on which the plaintiff allegedly slipped was created by water dripping from the gutter on the defendant’s property
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted the defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
